clue.text: Old Spanish commander in chief ran corporation

indicators.note: the letter wanted sits inside the following word rather than being its meaning, so just one of its letters is kept

blocks.note: the closing letter of this word
taken as written
Co. is the standard abbreviation for company or corporation

explanation.surface: A history note: an old Spanish commander-in-chief who went on to run a corporation.
explanation.walkthrough: The parse is loose: 'commander in chief' reads as one phrase, but only 'Old Spanish commander' defines, and the first letter comes from inside 'chief'. General Francisco Franco ruled Spain from 1939 to 1975.
explanation.definitionFit: Francisco Franco was the Spanish general who led the Nationalist army and then ruled as dictator.

clue.text: On the up, scoundrel and guru, male icon

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the letters read from bottom to top, the opposite way

blocks.note: a rat is a contemptible, treacherous person
a guru is a wise teacher, a sage
M is the standard abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A rising star who is both a rogue and a spiritual teacher, an idol to his fans.
explanation.walkthrough: RAT, SAGE and M are strung together and then the whole string is flipped, since this is a down light read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An icon in the celebrity sense is a hugely famous performer, which is exactly what a megastar is.

clue.text: Standard beach costume, looks to cover it

indicators.note: to cover something is to go around it, so one word wraps itself about the rest

blocks.note: stares are long looks
a beach is made of sand
a strip is a team's sports outfit, its kit

explanation.surface: People ogle a swimsuit on the beach, and it is a standard design.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' is a flag, not a norm. SAND and STRIP go inside STARES, and 'it' points back at the beach costume. In Britain a strip is a sports team's kit.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is a flag or banner, and the Stars and Stripes is the national flag of the United States.

clue.text: Bangladesh’s opening bat – one of those offering support

indicators.note: an opening is a start, so only the first letter of the name is wanted

blocks.note: first letter of the country name
a racket is the bat used in tennis or squash

explanation.surface: Bangladesh's opening batsman, one of the players who backs up the team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening bat' sounds like cricket's first batsman, but 'opening' takes the first letter and 'bat' is a racket.
explanation.definitionFit: A bracket is a wall fixture that holds up a shelf, so it is one of many things that support a load.

blocks.note: surface reading: a monarch sitting in a baby's cot, put briefly
setter's reading: the capitals CRI begin the word, and C R I is the short royal monogram of Carolus Rex the First

explanation.surface: A baby king lying in his cot, described in a word.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals are the clue: C.R. (Carolus Rex) plus I is how this Stuart king abbreviated his title, and those letters open CRIB. He reigned 1625 to 1649 and was beheaded.
explanation.definitionFit: The royal cipher CR I stands for Carolus Rex Primus, Latin for the first king named Charles.

definitions.note: a cryptic description of a hat, a noun

blocks.note: first meaning: the Central American nation
second meaning: a straw hat, something that goes on the head

explanation.walkthrough: 'Going to one's head' sounds like getting conceited or drunk; here it is literal, an item worn on the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Panama is a nation on the isthmus joining the Americas, and a panama is a lightweight woven straw hat.

indicators.note: the answer lies inside the run of words that follows, spanning a word break

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A cricket bowler delivers underarm in a Test match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowl over' and 'underarm' suggest cricket bowling, but the definition is the idiom for amazing someone. A Test is an international cricket match.
explanation.definitionFit: To be bowled over is to be astonished or overwhelmed, the same effect as being stunned by news.

clue.text: Cheese in salty water, name forgotten

indicators.note: something forgotten is left out, so a letter is dropped from the word

blocks.note: brine is water with salt in it
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Cheese kept in brine, with its label lost.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the N for 'name' out of BRINE. 'In' looks like part of the picture of cheese soaking, but it is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Brie is a soft French cow's-milk cheese with an edible white rind.

indicators.note: something rolled over is flipped end to end, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: rot is decay

explanation.surface: A boulder sunk in decay has toppled over.
explanation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky outcrop on a hilltop, common on Dartmoor in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A tor is a craggy hill or pile of rock, so it serves as a plain synonym for rock.

clue.text: Those that beat Scottish football team

blocks.note: first meaning: the organs that pump blood with a regular beat
second meaning: Heart of Midlothian, the Edinburgh club

explanation.surface: The sides that defeated a Scottish football club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Those that beat' reads as the winners of a match; it is the organs that beat. Heart of Midlothian is an Edinburgh football club known as Hearts.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearts are the organs whose pulse beats, and Hearts is the everyday nickname of Heart of Midlothian FC.

indicators.note: doing something ludicrously means in an absurd, disordered way, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
to air a programme is to broadcast it

explanation.surface: A complaint that some silly entertainment on TV was shocking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' could be an anagram signal; here it is AIR, and only FUN is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Outrageous in the sense of shockingly unjust, as in an outrageous decision, matches unfair.

clue.text: Those hung and drawn in death?

blocks.note: first meaning: window drapes, which are hung up and drawn open or shut
second meaning: the slang for the end

explanation.surface: Traitors hanged, drawn and quartered in an execution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hung and drawn' calls up the old punishment of hanging, drawing and quartering, but the things hung and drawn are window drapes.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying it is curtains for someone is an idiom meaning their end or death has come.

blocks.note: first meaning: a scornful retort to a ridiculous claim
second meaning: a literal plea to someone who keeps amusing you

explanation.surface: Someone helpless with giggles begs a joker to stop.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works both as a sneer of disbelief and, read literally, as a request to stop being funny.
explanation.definitionFit: The expression is idiomatic scorn meaning a suggestion is absurd, and literally a plea not to cause laughter.

blocks.note: first meaning: a joke
second meaning: to stop someone speaking

explanation.surface: A strange thing, this sudden silence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny thing' sounds like an odd event; it means a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A gag is a comedian's joke, and to gag someone is to prevent them speaking, physically or legally.

clue.text: Sat casually, travel with a leg either side

indicators.note: doing something casually means doing it loosely and without order, so the letters fall out of place

blocks.note: taken as written
to ride is to travel on a horse or vehicle

explanation.surface: A rider sits loosely in the saddle, legs on both flanks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sat casually' looks like a relaxed posture; 'casually' only rearranges SAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Sitting astride a horse or bicycle means having one leg on each side of it.

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading from bottom to top, the reverse direction

blocks.note: nos is the abbreviation for numbers; the letters also happen to run forwards across 'numbers on', a coincidence

explanation.surface: Figures on relatives are climbing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relative numbers' suggests ratios; 'Relative' is the definition and 'numbers' gives the abbreviation NOS.
explanation.definitionFit: A son is a male child, one of a person's closest family members.

blocks.note: first meaning: free and on the loose, like an escaped prisoner
second meaning: as a whole

explanation.walkthrough: Two senses of one phrase: escaped and free, or taken as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: An escaped convict at large is roaming free, and the public at large means people in general.

clue.text: One suit with king turned up in card trick

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned upwards means the letters run bottom to top, backwards
one group of letters is placed inside another word

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
to suit is to fit
R for rex, Latin for king
an ace is a playing card

explanation.surface: A conjuror's card trick in which a king of one suit turns face up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Card trick' reads as one phrase, but 'card' supplies letters and 'trick' alone is the definition. R for king comes from Latin rex.
explanation.definitionFit: Artifice is clever deception or a cunning device, so a trick is one instance of it.

clue.text: Go off track on your bike!

blocks.note: first meaning: stray from the route
second meaning: British slang telling someone to go away

explanation.surface: A cyclist wanders off the path, and someone shouts at them to ride on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On your bike!' is British slang for 'go away', not advice about cycling.
explanation.definitionFit: To get lost is to stray off course, and 'get lost!' is a rude dismissal like 'clear off'.

blocks.note: first meaning: feeling poorly
second meaning: literally beneath the weather as it falls

explanation.surface: Out in a storm, getting soaked and battered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rough' fits the stormy picture but means unwell, a British usage as in 'I feel rough'.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling under the weather is an idiom for being mildly ill, and being rained on puts you literally beneath it.

indicators.note: something faked is made up or forged, so the letters are reworked into a new word

blocks.note: the letters of these words, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: An inventor caught using a forged identity card.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Edison was the American inventor of the phonograph and a practical light bulb.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Alva Edison held over a thousand patents and is the archetypal example of an inventor.

blocks.note: first meaning: listen in secretly, as a hidden microphone does
second meaning: the pincered garden creature

explanation.surface: Deploy a bug, an actual insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' seems to mean the insect, but here it is a listening device; to earwig is British slang for eavesdropping.
explanation.definitionFit: To earwig is to eavesdrop as a hidden microphone does, and an earwig is a small insect with rear pincers.

clue.text: Stamped rubbish bags in courtyard identified, initially

indicators.note: to bag is to hold in a sack, so one word encloses other letters
initially means at the start, so only the opening letters of the words are kept

blocks.note: offal is waste or refuse, the discarded parts of a carcass
first letter of each word

explanation.surface: Someone stamped on rubbish bags found in a yard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stamped' reads as trampling, but it means bearing an authority's stamp; 'rubbish' is waste meat rather than refuse sacks.
explanation.definitionFit: A stamped document carries an authorised seal, which makes it official, approved by the proper authority.

blocks.note: first meaning: dull and lifeless
second meaning: an apartment

explanation.surface: A dull spot to make one's home.
explanation.walkthrough: A flat is the British word for an apartment.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat performance is dull and lacks spirit, and a flat is a set of rooms forming a home.

indicators.note: in an across entry, one thing on another comes after it, so the first-named piece is placed second

blocks.note: a batsman who is batting is in
a form is an official document to fill in

explanation.surface: A short memo on how the cricket batting went.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' looks like an adjective for the document but is a verb. In cricket the side currently batting is said to be 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: To brief someone is to give them the facts they need, which is to inform them.

blocks.note: a cap is a kind of hat
something worn is on
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: The hat sported by a British mobster.
explanation.walkthrough: Al Capone ran organised crime in Prohibition-era Chicago, though he was American, not English.
explanation.definitionFit: Al Capone was the notorious Chicago mob boss of the 1920s, the most famous gangster of all.

clue.text: 16 Down turns out to be female relative

indicators.note: to turn someone out is to throw them out, so part of the word is ejected

blocks.note: the answer to that clue
is is a form of the verb to be

explanation.surface: A son who turns out to be a sister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turns out to be' wants to be a single phrase, but it splits: the 'on' that turns are switched to is removed, and 'to be' supplies a verb form.
explanation.definitionFit: Sis is the informal shortening of sister, a female sibling and so a female relative.

definitions.note: the shot a golfer plays with a wedge

blocks.note: first meaning: a fried potato stick
second meaning: in golf a wedge is a club used for a short lofted shot

explanation.surface: Asking what a potato wedge is used for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wedge' does double duty: a chunky fried potato, and the golf club for lifting a short shot onto the green.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain chips are fried potato pieces, and a chip shot in golf is a short lofted stroke played with a wedge.
